chunks: From him, from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a woman who swore by freeing her slave girl or by walking to the House of God that she would never go out to her husband, while he was in a land other than the one she was in. He did not send her maintenance, and she had a great need and could not provide for herself. He said: 'Indeed, although she is angry, she swore where she swore, and she intends to go out to him willingly, and she is able to do so. If she knew that this was not appropriate for her, she would not have sworn. So let her go out to her husband, and there is no penalty upon her for her oath, for this is more righteous.'

key_terms.بِالْمَشْيِ إِلَى بَيْتِ اللَّهِ: By walking to the House of God

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a woman who swore to stay away from her husband if he didn't send maintenance, but he didn't send it and she needed it?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) clarifies the nature of a woman's oath to remain separated from her husband due to withheld maintenance. He rules that since her intention was to enforce her right rather than permanently sever ties, the oath is binding but does not require expiation (*kaffarah*) upon fulfillment, as her anger justified the vow. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that oaths taken in anger or for legitimate rights are often treated with leniency regarding expiation if the underlying intent was not permanent separation.
